---
title: "Lagrangian perturbation theory to fourth order"
---

## Beyond Zel'dovich

The Zel'dovich approximation @eq-za ignores the right-hand side of the
equation of motion @eq-eom-D beyond linear order: fluid elements are never
accelerated by the structure they form. **Lagrangian perturbation theory**
(LPT) fixes this order by order with the ansatz

$$
\boldsymbol\Psi(\mathbf q, D) = \sum_{n\ge1} D^n\,\boldsymbol\Psi^{(n)}(\mathbf q),
$$ {#eq-lpt-series}

where $\boldsymbol\Psi^{(1)} = -\nabla\varphi$ is the Zel'dovich term. The
$D^n$ time dependence is exact in an Einstein–de Sitter universe and an
excellent approximation otherwise (the exact $\Lambda$CDM growth functions
differ from $D^n$ by at most a few per cent, which is why the laboratory uses
the EdS form; DISCO-DJ and similar codes offer both).

## The equations in Lagrangian form

Take the divergence and the curl of @eq-eom-D in Eulerian coordinates and
transform to $\mathbf q$ using $\partial/\partial x_j = J^{-1} C_{ji}\,\partial/\partial q_i$
with the cofactor matrix $C$ of $\partial\mathbf x/\partial\mathbf q$. With the
shorthand $M_{ab} = \partial_b\Psi_a$ and the operator
$\mathcal R = \partial_D^2 + \tfrac{3}{2D}\partial_D$, the two equations
are

$$
C_{ji}\,\partial_i(\mathcal R\Psi_j) = -\frac{3}{2D^2}\,(1 - J)
\qquad\text{(longitudinal: Poisson)}
$$ {#eq-lpt-long}

$$
\varepsilon_{ijk}\,\dot x_{l,j}\,x_{l,k} = 0
\qquad\text{(transverse: zero vorticity, Cauchy invariants)}
$$ {#eq-lpt-trans}

Because $\mathcal R(D^n) = n(n+\tfrac12)D^{n-2}$ and the right-hand side of
@eq-lpt-long is a polynomial in the $M^{(n)}$, collecting powers of $D$
gives a closed recursion. For order $n \ge 2$ [@rampf2021; see also @zheligovsky2014; @matsubara2015; @schmidt2021; @michaux2021]:

$$
\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\Psi^{(n)} = \sum_{a+b=n} c_2(n;a,b)\,\mu_2\!\big(M^{(a)},M^{(b)}\big)
+ \sum_{a+b+c=n} c_3(n;a,b,c)\,\mu_3\!\big(M^{(a)},M^{(b)},M^{(c)}\big),
$$ {#eq-lpt-rec-long}

$$
\nabla\times\boldsymbol\Psi^{(n)} = -\frac1n \sum_{m=1}^{n-1} m\;
\varepsilon_{ijk}\,M^{(m)}_{lj}\,M^{(n-m)}_{lk},
$$ {#eq-lpt-rec-trans}

with the coefficients

$$
c_2 = \frac{\tfrac{3-n}{2} - a^2 - b^2}{(n+\tfrac32)(n-1)},\qquad
c_3 = \frac{\tfrac{3-n}{2} - a^2 - b^2 - c^2}{(n+\tfrac32)(n-1)},
$$

sums over ordered tuples, and the polarized invariants
$\mu_2(A,B) = \tfrac12[\operatorname{tr}A\operatorname{tr}B - \operatorname{tr}(AB)]$
and $\mu_3(A,B,C)$, the symmetric trilinear form with $\mu_3(A,A,A) = \det A$.
The divergence and curl determine $\boldsymbol\Psi^{(n)}$ uniquely in
Fourier space: $\hat{\boldsymbol\Psi} = -i\mathbf k\,\hat S/k^2 + i\mathbf k\times\hat{\mathbf T}/k^2$.

::: {.callout-note title="Sanity checks"}
* $n = 2$: $c_2(2;1,1) = -3/7$ and $\mu_2(M^{(1)},M^{(1)}) =
  \tfrac12[(\nabla^2\varphi)^2 - \varphi_{,ij}\varphi_{,ij}]$: the classic
  2LPT result $\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol\Psi^{(2)} = -\tfrac37\sum_{i<j}(\varphi_{,ii}\varphi_{,jj} - \varphi_{,ij}^2)$.
* $n = 3$: the coefficients $-1/3$ ($\mu_3$), $10/21$ ($\mu_2$ of orders 1 and
  2) and $1/7$ (transverse) of @bouchet1995 are recovered.
* The transverse part vanishes at orders 1 and 2 and is first non-zero at
  third order: LPT displacements are *not* potential beyond 2LPT even though
  the Eulerian velocity is.
* The laboratory's Rust implementation is verified by inserting the truncated
  series back into @eq-lpt-long and @eq-lpt-trans: the residuals scale as
  $D^{n+1}$ and $D^{n}$ respectively for $n = 1,\dots,4$, in both 2D and 3D.
:::

### Two dimensions

The laboratory's fast mode is two-dimensional. We treat it as a 3D universe
with translational symmetry along $z$: all fields depend on $(x, y)$ only,
all $z$-derivatives vanish, and the 3D equations above apply verbatim with
$2\times2$ matrices ($\mu_3 \equiv 0$ and only the $z$-component of the curl
survives). The growth factors and all coefficients stay the same, so the
2D laboratory is quantitatively faithful to the 3D theory for planar
structures.

## From the series to a density

Given $\boldsymbol\Psi^{(n)}$ on a Lagrangian grid we evaluate
@eq-lpt-series at any $D$ (it is just a polynomial), move the grid points
and ask what the Eulerian density is. There are two standard answers:

**Particles.** Treat each grid point as a particle and deposit its mass on
an Eulerian mesh (nearest-grid-point, cloud-in-cell, ...). Simple and
dimension-agnostic, but noisy and biased by the assignment window.

**The phase-space sheet** [@abel2012]. The grid points are *vertices* of the sheet; the sheet itself is the
piecewise-linear interpolation between them. Split each Lagrangian cell into
two triangles (2D) or six tetrahedra (3D); each simplex carries a fixed mass
and its density is mass over current volume. The Eulerian density at a point
is the *sum over all simplices covering it*: this is @eq-density-jacobian
made discrete, multi-streaming included, with no free parameters and no
shot noise. The laboratory renders the triangles on the GPU with additive
blending, so you literally see the sheet fold.

```{=html}
<div class="hcc-widget" data-widget="lptorders"></div>
<script type="module" src="../app/js/widgets.js"></script>
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it: order by order"}
The panel shows the 2D sheet density for the same Gaussian field evolved to
the same $D$ with 1LPT (Zel'dovich), 2LPT, 3LPT and 4LPT, together with the
divergence source of each order. Second order deepens voids and sharpens
filaments; third and fourth orders are small corrections *before* shell
crossing and grow rapidly after it. The series converges up to the first
shell crossing and (in a precise sense made rigorous by @zheligovsky2014 and
@rampf2021) not beyond, which is why we restrict the
quantitative comparisons to $D < D_{\rm sc}$.
:::

## The smoothing scale

Every realization in the laboratory starts from a Gaussian field smoothed
with a filter $e^{-k^2R^2/2}$. Three different reasons make this
unavoidable, and keeping them apart matters:

1. **Resolution.** Products of fields on a grid alias power above the Nyquist
   frequency back onto the resolved modes; a cutoff well below Nyquist (or
   zero-padding) keeps the recursion clean.
2. **Convergence.** Shell crossing happens first on the smallest scales. The
   larger the small-scale power, the earlier $D_{\rm sc}$ and the smaller the
   window in which perturbation theory is valid at all.
3. **Physics.** On small scales cold dark matter is genuinely multi-stream
   and *no* fluid description applies. The effective field theory of
   large-scale structure ([Chapter 7](07-mode-coupling.qmd)) takes the
   dependence on the cutoff seriously and absorbs it into measurable
   parameters.

The smoothing scale is a slider in the laboratory precisely so that you can
watch all three effects. The dimensionless combination that controls
everything is the rms displacement over the smoothing length,
$D\,\sigma_\Psi / R$.
